A seminary is a school — but not just any school. It is a specialized institution whose entire purpose is to train people to become religious leaders. Think of it as a college dedicated specifically to preparing priests, pastors, ministers, rabbis, imams, or other clergy for a life of religious service.

When you hear "seminary" in modern usage, this is almost always what it means: a religious training institution.

Suppose someone feels a deep calling to become a Catholic priest, a Protestant pastor, or a Jewish rabbi. After their regular college education, they would typically attend a seminary to receive formal, structured training for that role. The seminary teaches them:

  • Theology — the academic study of religion, religious doctrine, and the nature of God
  • Scripture — deep study of sacred texts (the Bible, the Torah, the Quran, etc.)
  • Religious history and philosophy
  • Practical ministry skills — how to preach, lead worship, counsel people in personal crisis, perform religious ceremonies (weddings, funerals), and guide a community in matters of faith

What makes a seminary different from a regular university is its singular focus. A university trains people for many different careers. A seminary exists for one purpose only: shaping someone into a religious leader. It is as much about personal spiritual formation — developing the character, values, and inner life suitable for a religious vocation — as it is about academic knowledge. Many seminaries do award formal academic degrees (a common one is the Master of Divinity, or M.Div.), but the goal is not just an academic qualification; it is the full preparation of a person to serve as a minister of religion.

Examples:

  • "After years of spiritual reflection, he left his career in law and enrolled in a seminary to train for the priesthood."
  • "The seminary requires its students to spend time in local communities, not just in classrooms."
  • "She graduated from the seminary with a Master of Divinity and was ordained as a pastor the following year."

In the 18th and 19th centuries — especially in the United States and Britain — the word "seminary" was also widely used to describe a private secondary school for young women, often called a "female seminary" or "ladies' seminary." These schools had nothing necessarily to do with religion; they simply offered academic education to girls at a time when most formal schooling was designed for boys.

This meaning has largely disappeared from everyday modern English. You will not hear someone use "seminary" this way today. However, if you are reading older literature, historical documents, or books from that era, you will likely come across it. When you do, it means a girls' school or academy — not a religious institution.

Example from this older context:

  • "At the age of fourteen, she was sent to a female seminary in the city, where she studied literature, arithmetic, music, and French."
A figurative use (found in older or formal writing)

Occasionally, in classical literature or formal prose, "seminary" is used figuratively — meaning not as a literal school, but as a way of saying that a place or situation is a source or breeding ground for something. It is used in the pattern: "a seminary of [something]."

This usage is rare in everyday modern speech, but you may encounter it in older texts.

Examples:

  • "He called the city a seminary of vice and corruption."
  • "The great university was regarded as a seminary of revolutionary ideas."

In these cases, the writer is not talking about an actual school. They are simply saying that this place produces and nurtures that quality, in the same way that a school produces graduates.

The word "seminary" has three layers, ordered by how often you will encounter them today:

1. Most common — a religious training school: A specialized institution where people study theology and religious practice to become priests, pastors, rabbis, or other religious leaders. This is what the word means almost every time you encounter it in modern life.

2. Historical — a girls' school: A private school for young women, common in the 18th and 19th centuries. This meaning is largely obsolete now but appears frequently in older literature.

3. Figurative — a source or breeding ground: Used in formal or literary writing to describe any place that produces or cultivates people or ideas of a certain kind.

The thread connecting all three meanings is the same: a seminary, in every sense, is a place that produces or forms something — whether that is religious leaders, educated young women, or ideas.
